newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese queue for last batch of 1996 T-bonds.
newsitem.headline: Chinese queue for last batch of 1996 T-bonds.

text.p: Chinese on Friday queued to buy the last batch of treasury bonds issued this year, but underwriters holding them sold only a small portion -- believing that falling inflation makes them an excellent investment.

China's first seven-year T-bonds went on sale on Friday in offices of underwriters, including securities houses and banks. The bonds carried a coupon of 8.56 percent, 1.09 percentage points higher than the annual rate for one-year bank deposits.

In one Shanghai office of Shenyin and Wanguo Securities, the nation's largest brokerage, hundreds of investors stood in a long queue, with the firm limiting each buyer to 1,000 yuan ($120) worth of the bonds, witnesses said.
The branches of many banks which underwrote part of the issue did not offer any bonds to sell despite queues there before opening time, witnesses said.
"Investors believe the coupon of this batch of bonds is high because bank interest rates are likely to come down again next year due to falling inflation," one T-bond trader said.
"In addition, the bonds have the advantage that the interest is paid on an annual basis and they are tradeable after the issue," he said.
Interest for the new bond will be calculated as from November 1 and will be paid on an annual basis instead of at maturity, allowing buyers to re-invest.

A total of 20 billion yuan ($2.41 billion) worth of the bonds are being issued from Friday, to November 20. They will be listed on November 21 on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges after the issue.
This is the first time that China has issued seven-year T-bonds and Shanghai securities analysts said the period is designed to suit China's economic development cycle.
Analysts said that both the underwriters and the individual investor queuing in the rain were betting that the bond's interest rate would be higher than bank interest rates in the foreseeable future.

China's central bank cut bank interest rates twice this year after sharp falls in retail price inflation, which is expected to hit a year-on-year six percent this year from a year-on-year 14.8 percent last year.
"Chinese financial institutions have become major holders of state debt due to a series of reform by the central government this year," said a securities investment analyst.
"In the past, they were allocated certain amounts of T-bonds and tried every means to sell them to individuals," he added.
"But most underwriters now intend to retain a lion's share in their hands," he said.
The bonds have become more attractive to the underwriters because of efforts by Beijing to make the issue of T-bonds this year more market-oriented, analysts said.

The bulk of bonds have been given to underwriters on the basis of public tenders instead of by administrative edict, as in the past. Prices have largely been set by the market through these tenders instead of fixed by the ministry as before.
Beijing has encouraged development of the T-bond secondary markets, including repurchase and spot markets, by allowing most new issues to be listed and freely traded after the issue.
China planned to issue a record of 195.2 billion yuan worth of T-bills and T-bonds this year and, before the seven-year bond, nearly 180 billion yuan worth had been issued.
